comparison: Perfect alignment on limitations (C39, C40, C113-C115). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers support the acknowledgment of Python-only availability, performance limitations, and learning curve concerns. Peer reviewers note documentation adequately addresses these limitations.

Strong agreement on I/O layer capabilities (C21-C25, C77, C82-C85, C106). Both evaluations support the NWB format integration and multi-format import capabilities. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm the I/O layer addresses community needs.

Strong agreement on demonstration datasets (C44-C48, C62-C66, C88). Both evaluations support the versatility claims based on diverse reanalysis examples. Peer reviewers found the evidence compelling with live coding notebooks.

Both identify future work claims (C42-C43, C117-C119) as uncertain/speculative. OpenEval marks these as aspirational rather than demonstrated. Peer reviewers note minor uncertainty about backward compatibility claims (C34).

Strong agreement on core architecture (C2-C3, C11-C12, C32, C95, C100, C102). Both evaluations support Pynapple's object-oriented design and core data structures. Peer reviewers affirm this represents a valuable contribution.

Divergent evaluations on object-oriented benefits (C9-C10, C75-C76). OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN due to lack of empirical validation for error reduction claims. Peer reviewers explicitly SUPPORT the design approach, with Reviewer 1 affirming it simplifies analysis.

Strong agreement on Pynacollada separation strategy (C29-C31, C67-C68, C90, C92-C94, C110). Both evaluations support the modular architecture rationale. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm the separation for streamlined base and experimental approaches.

Strong agreement on foundational analytical capabilities (C26-C28, C49-C52, C80, C86-C87, C89, C96). Both evaluations support the core analysis methods. Peer reviewers note well-written analysis routines with compelling evidence.

Divergent evaluations on comparative claims (C38, C111-C112). OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN, noting lack of quantitative benchmarking. Peer reviewers SUPPORT the problem statement, with Reviewer 1 affirming authors identified a key community need.

Divergent evaluations on impact claims (C72-C74, C97, C99, C101). OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN, noting these are aspirational without empirical validation of adoption or reproducibility improvements. Peer reviewers SUPPORT these claims, affirming potential as valuable and foundational tools.

Divergent evaluations on dependency choices and stability (C33-C34, C41, C81, C103, C116). OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN due to speculative future stability claims. Peer reviewers SUPPORT the technical foundation with no criticism of implementation choices.

Strong agreement on scope and interoperability (C35-C37). Both evaluations support preprocessing assumptions and flexibility claims. Peer reviewers affirm multi-format import and NWB wrapper capabilities. OpenEval also addresses C104-C105 (FAIR principles) which peer reviewers cover in R11.

Overlap on specific analysis methods (C53-C60). OpenEval groups these with broader analytical capabilities (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers implicitly accept these technical features through lack of criticism and affirmation of well-written routines.
Partial overlap on contextual claims (C6-C8). OpenEval supports these as established field knowledge. Peer reviewers address these in context of affirming the problem statement and community need.

Partial overlap on Pandas inheritance (C13-C17). OpenEval groups these with core architecture as SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers implicitly accept technical foundation without specific commentary on inheritance details.
OpenEval addresses time_support rationale (C20) as SUPPORTED logical inference. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this design feature (grouped in R12) without specific commentary.
Minor overlap on time_support and default units (C18-C19). OpenEval groups with core architecture as SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these technical features without specific evaluation.

Minor overlap on design benefits (C78-C79). OpenEval marks object-oriented benefits as UNCERTAIN due to lack of empirical validation. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these through general affirmation of design approach.

Partial overlap on FAIR principles and interoperability (C104-C105). OpenEval supports these as reasonable inferences. Peer reviewers address community value more broadly, affirming contribution to the field.
Minor overlap on extensibility (C108). OpenEval supports this as reasonable design inference. Peer reviewers address flexibility and interoperability more broadly in R13.
Minor overlap on future stability (C34). OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN/speculative. Peer reviewers note minor uncertainty about backward compatibility phrasing but generally accept the claim.
OpenEval evaluates contextual/motivational claims (C1, C4-C5) as SUPPORTED by citations and established knowledge. No corresponding focused peer evaluation, though context is implicitly accepted.
